prompt: I'm the product lead at Northwind Boards, a collaborative whiteboard tool sold to teams of 5 to 200 seats. Leadership wants one top-line metric for the whole company starting January 2027. Right now every department reports something different. Sales watches seats sold, support watches ticket volume, and product watches daily active users, which sit around 18,000. About 62 percent of paying workspaces have at least three members who edited a board in the last 30 days. I'm assuming our customers get value from teams working on boards together rather than from individuals using the tool alone, but I haven't confirmed that with customer interviews. I also don't know whether our largest accounts behave differently from small teams, because we've never split the usage data that way. Can you help me choose a candidate metric, explain the reasoning, and suggest two or three supporting metrics that sit under it? This is for a one-page memo to our CEO, Jane Okafor, and our head of sales, so non-analysts need to be able to follow it.

I'm the solo product manager at Larkspoon, a new consumer recipe and meal-planning app. We launch on iOS in March 2027 with a 7-day free trial that rolls into an $8.99 monthly subscription. Our engineering lead, Ravi, has asked me for a written list of the events we should track from day one, so he can build tracking into the app rather than add it later. The core flows are onboarding with dietary preferences, browsing recipes, saving recipes, building a weekly meal plan, generating a shopping list, and the trial-to-paid paywall. I'm assuming most people will decide whether to subscribe near the end of the trial, around day 6 or 7, so I want to understand what they do before that point. One open question is whether we'll ship Android at launch or three months later. Leadership hasn't decided, and I don't want to design something that breaks across platforms. Please give me an event list with suggested names, the properties each event should carry, and a short note on why each one matters. Ravi and two engineers will build from this document directly.

I'm a growth analyst at Acme Outfitters, an online apparel retailer. We just finished a 21-day A/B test on the checkout page. The control had our usual grey 'Continue to payment' button. The variant used a larger green button with the label 'Pay securely now'. Each arm got roughly 48,200 visitors. Control converted at 3.10 percent and the variant at 3.24 percent. Our testing dashboard reports an 87 percent chance that the variant is better. I'm assuming the traffic split was clean and that nothing else on the site changed during the test, although I'd only call that likely, not confirmed. I haven't yet broken the results down by mobile versus desktop, and I don't know whether the effect holds on both. Our VP of e-commerce, Dana Whitfield, wants a recommendation by next Friday, October 23, on whether to ship the variant, keep testing, or drop it. Can you help me write that recommendation? I need the conclusion, how confident we should be, and any caveats she should know. She's sharp but not a statistician.

I lead growth at Pebble Budget, a personal finance app with a free tier and a paid tier. Since we started a paid social campaign in mid-August, weekly signups are up about 34 percent, from around 5,200 to 7,000. Week-four retention hasn't moved at all. It's been flat at roughly 21 percent for the cohorts from June through September. Our CMO, Theo Brandt, is pleased about the signup numbers but keeps asking why the extra users aren't showing up in active users. I'm assuming the new users are broadly similar to the people who signed up before the campaign, though I haven't checked. One thing I'm unsure about is whether the definition of a signup changed on September 2, when engineering added Google login. It's possible some accounts are now counted differently. I'd like help working out what to look at first and in what order, and which explanations are worth ruling in or out. I'll present this at our growth team meeting next Tuesday, and a short version will go to Theo afterwards.

I'm the product manager for onboarding at Quillstack, a note-taking app for students. We want to test a redesigned onboarding flow against the current one. About 1,400 new users sign up each week. Today 38 percent of them reach our activation point, which is creating three notes within their first seven days. Our roadmap review is on December 15, which gives us about eight weeks, and I'd like a result before then. I'm assuming weekly signups will stay roughly stable through November, although exam season might change that. I honestly don't know what size of improvement is realistic, because nobody here has tested onboarding before. The design lead, Priya Nair, believes the new flow could be a big win. My manager is skeptical that we have enough users to learn anything. Can you help me work out whether this test is feasible with our traffic, how long it would need to run, and what we should do if the numbers don't work? I need to share a short plan with Priya and my manager this week.

I'm the product manager at Tallyhouse, an invoicing tool for freelancers. We go from private beta to public launch on November 6, 2026, three weeks from today. Our beta has 340 users, and our tracking right now amounts to page views and a signup count. Engineering can give me about two developer-days for instrumentation before launch, so I can't have everything. Most launch traffic should come from a newsletter feature and a few partner announcements on the same day. I'm assuming launch week will bring a spike of curious visitors, followed by a much smaller steady stream. What I don't know is whether our investors will expect retention and revenue numbers at the January board meeting. If they do, anything we fail to capture now is gone for good. Please help me decide what to instrument before launch and what can wait, in priority order, with a sentence on why each item makes the cut. The list goes to our CTO, Marco Silva, who will scope the work on Monday.

I'm a product analyst at Fernhill Fitness, a workout app. We started a test on September 28 that changed the timing of our trial-reminder push notification. It was planned to run for four weeks. On day seven, our head of growth, Liam Archer, saw the dashboard showing an 11 percent lift in trial-to-paid conversion marked as significant, and he stopped the test. Each arm had about 9,800 users at that point. He now wants to roll the change out to everyone next week. I'm assuming that first week looked like a normal week for us. However, I'm not sure whether our October 1 to 3 sitewide discount affected one arm more than the other, or affected the results at all. I'd like help working out how far we can trust this result, what risks come with rolling it out now, and what, if anything, we should do before making the change permanent. I need to write this up for Liam in a way that is honest but doesn't read as obstructive, since he's under pressure to show wins this quarter.

I'm the head of product at Brightline Forms, a self-serve online form builder. Our leadership offsite is November 20, and we need to choose one primary team goal for Q1 2027. Annual recurring revenue is $4.2 million and grows about 3 percent per month. Activation, defined as creating and publishing a first form within seven days of signup, sits at 29 percent. The CFO, Amara Lindqvist, wants the goal to be revenue, because that is what the board tracks. Our CEO leans towards activation, because she thinks it is the bottleneck. Activated users convert to paid at about three times the rate of non-activated users. I'm assuming part of that relationship is causal, but I know some of it may simply reflect people who were already more motivated. I also don't know how long it takes for an activation gain to show up in revenue. It may take longer than a single quarter. Can you help me lay out the tradeoffs and make a recommendation? It needs to be a two-page pre-read for the CEO and CFO before the offsite.

I'm the lead analyst at Corrigan Travel, a trip-booking site. Our tracking has grown messy over four years. We now have 412 distinct event names. Many are duplicates with inconsistent naming, such as 'signup_completed', 'SignUp Complete' and 'user_signed_up', which all appear to describe the same moment. Some events also carry properties in mixed formats, for example prices recorded as strings in some places and as numbers in others. I'm assuming roughly a third of these events haven't fired in the last 90 days and can probably be retired, but I haven't run a full audit yet. The big unknown is which dashboards and reports depend on the old names. Finance in particular has built monthly reports that nobody on my team has reviewed. Can you help me plan the cleanup? I'd like a sequence of steps, a proposed naming convention, and an approach for migrating without breaking existing reports. The audience is our data engineering team and the six analysts who use this data daily. We'd like the migration finished by March 31, 2027.

I'm the pricing manager at Hollins Desk, a scheduling tool for small and mid-size businesses. We ran a five-week pricing test that ended October 3, raising our Starter plan from $12 to $15 per seat per month for half of new visitors. Among small businesses with fewer than 10 employees, trial-to-paid conversion fell from 6.8 percent to 5.9 percent. Among mid-size businesses, it rose from 4.1 percent to 4.6 percent. Overall revenue per visitor rose about 4 percent. The small-business group had roughly 11,000 visitors in the test, and the mid-size group had about 2,300. Company size comes from a self-reported field at signup, and I'm assuming it is reasonably accurate. I'm not sure whether the mid-size increase is real or noise, given the smaller sample. I need to write up the results for our pricing committee meeting on October 29. They will decide whether to keep the new price, roll it back, or try something else. Can you help me structure the report and say what we can and can't conclude from this?
